missions.title: Welcome to CyberCity
missions.briefing: Welcome, {player}. Every connection is a choice. Our city needs people who pause, verify, and help others do the same. Your patrol begins with a simple habit.
missions.objective: Learn the city controls and choose the first response to an unexpected request.
missions.takeaway: {player}, pause before acting on an unexpected request. Verify it through an official channel you already trust. The Internet Cafe is now open.

questions.prompt: A message says your student account will close in ten minutes. What is your first move?
options: Use the message link before time runs out.
Open the official portal using your saved bookmark.
Send the sender your password to confirm your identity.
questions.explanation: Urgency is a pressure tactic. Verify through a channel you choose independently.

questions.prompt: How do you begin a mission with a mentor in CyberCity?
options: Approach the mentor and press E.
Click a real website in your browser.
Send a message to another player.
questions.explanation: Use WASD or arrow keys to move, then press E near a mentor. J opens your journal; M opens the map.

missions.title: Small habits, strong defenses
missions.briefing: {player}, i used to reuse one password everywhere. Then one leaked account put all my others at risk. Help me build a better routine before we investigate the cafe inbox.
missions.objective: Choose safer habits for passwords, verification codes, and software updates.
missions.takeaway: {player}, use a unique password for each account, enable MFA, keep software updated, and never share one-time verification codes.

questions.prompt: Which password habit limits damage if one service is breached?
options: Reuse a long password on every service.
Use your birth date with a symbol.
Use unique passwords stored in a password manager.
questions.explanation: Unique passwords prevent one stolen password from opening multiple accounts.

questions.prompt: Someone claiming to be support asks for your one-time sign-in code. What should you do?
options: Send it if they know your name.
Refuse, end the conversation, and contact official support.
Post the code in the group chat.
questions.explanation: A verification code can approve account access. Do not share it, even with someone who claims to be support.

questions.prompt: Why install security updates from the official software source?
options: They fix known weaknesses that attackers may exploit.
They make every attachment safe.
They replace the need for backups.
questions.explanation: Updates repair known flaws. Backups, cautious behavior, and account protection still matter.

missions.title: The urgent inbox
missions.briefing: {player}, this message arrived in our student inbox. It looks official at first glance, but something feels wrong. Inspect the sender, request, and destination before deciding what to do.
missions.objective: Highlight all three suspicious indicators in the message and choose a safe response.
missions.takeaway: {player}, check the actual sender and destination. Treat urgency and password requests as warning signs. Report the message, then verify through an official channel.

questions.prompt: The evidence points to phishing. What should Maya do next?
options: Reply with her password to ask whether it is real.
Open the link to inspect the sign-in form.
Report the message and verify through her saved school portal.
questions.explanation: Reporting helps others. Independent verification avoids trusting the same suspicious message.

missions.subject: ACTION REQUIRED: account suspension
missions.document: Hello student, your access will be suspended. Review the details below.

evidence.label: 01 / SENDER
evidence.explanation:
LOOKALIKE SENDER

The cafe knows the official school domain is academy.example. This different domain needs independent verification. A display name proves nothing.

evidence.label: 02 / DEADLINE
evidence.explanation:
PRESSURE TACTIC

A very short deadline pushes you to skip checks. Slow down and verify through the official portal.

evidence.label: 03 / REQUEST
evidence.explanation:
CREDENTIAL REQUEST

The message directs you to a different domain to enter a password. Use a known bookmark instead.

evidence.label: 04 / GREETING
evidence.explanation:
CONTEXT, NOT PROOF

A generic greeting alone cannot decide whether a message is malicious. Judge the sender, destination, and request together.

missions.title: A convincing imitation
missions.briefing: {player}, the cafe received a link to a scholarship page. The logo looks familiar. Investigate the address and the form. The real scholarship service is scholarships.academy.example.
missions.objective: Inspect the fictional browser, identify three suspicious indicators, and classify the page.
missions.takeaway: {player}, read the full domain, not just the logo. HTTPS protects a connection but does not prove the site is honest. A scholarship should not ask for your email password. The Linux Lab is now open.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion is supported by the evidence?
options: This is a fake scholarship page. Leave it and report the URL.
The lock symbol proves the organization is trustworthy.
A familiar logo makes the password request reasonable.
questions.explanation: The mismatched domain and unnecessary password request outweigh the familiar branding.

missions.subject: Academy Scholarship Portal
missions.document: Congratulations! Your training scholarship is ready to claim.

evidence.label: 01 / DOMAIN
evidence.explanation:
WRONG DOMAIN

The trusted service is scholarships.academy.example. This is a separate lookalike domain, not a subdomain of academy.example.

evidence.label: 02 / FORM
evidence.explanation:
EXCESSIVE DATA REQUEST

A scholarship claim should not need the password to your email account. Never submit it here.

evidence.label: 03 / PROMISE
evidence.explanation:
REWARD AND URGENCY

An unexpected guaranteed reward plus an artificial deadline is a reason to pause and verify.

evidence.label: 04 / TRANSPORT
evidence.explanation:
ENCRYPTED DOES NOT MEAN HONEST

HTTPS encrypts traffic to this domain. A deceptive site can also use HTTPS. Verify who owns the destination.

missions.title: Three flags, three investigations
missions.briefing: {player}, each training filesystem hides a different clue. Explore an archive, investigate failed sign-ins, then restore the minimum file permission. Type help whenever you need a command reference.
missions.objective: Find and submit one flag in each of the three challenge filesystems.
missions.takeaway: {player}, investigate before acting. Hidden files, focused log searches and owner-only read permissions each reveal a different kind of evidence. The Web Security Lab is now open.

missions.title: Who owns this record?
missions.briefing: {player}, a training API checks that you are signed in, but forgets to check whose record you requested. Observe the flaw in our fictional profile service, then switch to defense.
missions.objective: Request training profile 1002 while signed in as Alex (1001), then select a server-side defense.
missions.takeaway: {player}, iDOR is an authorization failure. Every server request must verify that the current user is allowed to access the requested object. Hiding IDs in the interface is not sufficient.

questions.prompt: What removes the cause of this IDOR flaw?
options: Hide the profile ID in the page.
Rename the API endpoint.
Verify record ownership or an allowed role on the server for every request.
questions.explanation: Server-side object authorization must run for each request. A signed-in user is not entitled to every object.

missions.title: When text becomes markup
missions.briefing: {player}, an unsafe comment page can confuse user text with page markup. Use a harmless formatting marker to model the problem. The training preview is inert and runs no scripts.
missions.objective: Submit a harmless markup marker and choose the defense for untrusted output.
missions.takeaway: {player}, treat user content as data. Encode output for its destination context, use safe rendering APIs, and sanitize deliberately allowed markup with a maintained allowlist.

questions.prompt: Which defense addresses untrusted comments rendered into a page?
options: Encode output for the context and use safe text rendering.
Block only the word script.
Trust comments from signed-in users.
questions.explanation: Context-aware output encoding and safe rendering prevent text from being interpreted as code or markup.

missions.title: Keep data out of the query
missions.briefing: {player}, this fictional sign-in builds a database query by joining strings. Observe how a training input could alter its structure. No database is connected to this exercise.
missions.objective: Inspect the simulated query and choose a defense that separates commands from values.
missions.takeaway: {player}, use parameterized queries with bound values. This keeps user data separate from SQL structure. Input validation and limited database permissions add further protection.

questions.prompt: What is the primary defense against this SQL injection flaw?
options: Remove spaces from every input.
Use parameterized queries and bind input as values.
Use a hidden login form.
questions.explanation: Bound parameters keep values separate from query syntax. Filters and hidden interfaces do not provide that separation.

missions.title: Connect the evidence
missions.briefing: {player}, you have seen three weaknesses in isolation. Now explain the pattern from evidence, without guessing or touching external systems. Each finding must lead to a concrete defense.
missions.objective: Match three observations to IDOR, XSS, and SQL injection.
missions.takeaway: {player}, a useful finding connects the trigger, unauthorized effect, and root cause. Test only within authorized scope, then pair every finding with a defense. Blue is ready to help.

questions.prompt: Alex changes a training record number and receives Mira's private record. What failed?
options: The color of the login button.
Server-side object authorization (IDOR).
The image compression setting.
questions.explanation: A different object ID should not bypass the ownership check on the server.

questions.prompt: A comment is interpreted as page markup instead of being displayed as text. What class of risk does this model?
options: Cross-site scripting (XSS).
A weak Wi-Fi signal.
A missing backup.
questions.explanation: Untrusted text entering an executable rendering context can lead to XSS. Use safe rendering and context-aware encoding.

questions.prompt: User input changes the meaning of a dynamically joined database query. What is the flaw?
options: IDOR.
Phishing.
SQL injection.
questions.explanation: The query mixed data with command syntax. Parameterized queries separate them.

missions.title: Repair the trust boundaries
missions.briefing: {player}, a finding becomes valuable when we can fix it. Choose a mitigation for each root cause. Defense is more than hiding a symptom: the trust boundary must be enforced.
missions.objective: Choose a defense for authorization, output rendering, and database access.
missions.takeaway: {player}, enforce authorization on the server, encode untrusted output for its context, and bind database parameters. Retest fixes, update dependencies, and monitor for suspicious activity.

questions.prompt: Which patch should protect GET /api/profile/{id}?
options: Require login, then allow every numeric ID.
Hide the request from browser tools.
Check the caller's ownership or allowed role before returning the record.
questions.explanation: Authentication identifies a caller. Authorization checks what that caller may access.

questions.prompt: Which approach is safest when displaying an untrusted comment as plain text?
options: Insert it with a safe text API and context-aware output encoding.
Join it directly into HTML.
Reject only lowercase tags.
questions.explanation: A safe text sink treats the comment as data rather than interpreting it as markup.

questions.prompt: Which query approach keeps the username separate from SQL syntax?
options: Concatenate it after removing spaces.
Use a prepared statement with a bound username parameter.
Let the browser build the database query.
questions.explanation: Prepared statements with bound parameters preserve the intended query structure.

missions.title: The citywide incident
missions.briefing: {player}, the city receives a scholarship email leading to a fake portal. A separate training API exposes records, and unsafe query construction appears in the logs. Coordinate a response using everything you learned.
missions.objective: Verify the message, investigate the file evidence, identify the API flaw, and select the repair plan.
missions.takeaway: {player}, a complete response verifies sources, contains exposure, preserves evidence, fixes root causes, and retests. Report what happened clearly so the next citizen can avoid the same trap.

questions.prompt: The scholarship email links to academy-awards.example. The known portal is scholarships.academy.example. What comes first?
options: Sign in to see whether the form works.
Open the known portal independently and report the suspicious message.
Forward it to everyone to ask for help.
questions.explanation: Independent verification avoids trusting the suspicious message or spreading its link.

questions.prompt: An audit clue is in a hidden folder. Which sequence reveals it without executing unknown files?
options: ls -a, cd into the folder, then cat the evidence file.
Run every file until a flag appears.
Enter your password into the evidence file.
questions.explanation: List, navigate, and read. Investigation does not require executing unknown files.

questions.prompt: A signed-in user receives another person's record after changing its ID. Which repair matters?
options: A new logo.
A secret URL.
Server-side authorization for the requested record.
questions.explanation: Enforce object access on the server for every request, regardless of how the interface presents it.

questions.prompt: Which plan addresses the unsafe comments and concatenated queries, then verifies the repair?
options: Hide both forms and consider the case closed.
Use context-aware output encoding and bound parameters, then retest and monitor.
Ask users to avoid punctuation.
questions.explanation: Fix the rendering and query trust boundaries. Retest the same conditions and monitor for recurrence.

missions.title: A citizen worth trusting
missions.briefing: {player}, you followed the evidence, practiced the tools, and repaired the causes. The final lesson is a habit you can use every day: make trust a decision, not an assumption.
missions.objective: Choose the response that combines verification, privacy, and reporting.
missions.takeaway: {player}, patrol complete. You are a CyberCity citizen defender. Pause, verify independently, protect your accounts, and help others recognize the warning signs.

questions.prompt: An unexpected message asks for your login code to claim an urgent reward. Which habit will you carry forward?
options: Pause, withhold the code, verify independently, and report the message.
Trust it if the logo looks familiar.
Share the code if the reward is valuable.
questions.explanation: Verification, limited disclosure, and reporting work together to protect both you and your community.
